questions.question: Describe the site and situation of the Port of Durban and explain how it developed.
questions.expected_answer: The port lies on the east coast in eThekwini, KwaZulu-Natal, on the Indian Ocean. Its site is the Bay of Natal, a large natural bay sheltered by the Bluff, a high vegetated dune ridge, and the Point sandspit, giving calm water rare on South Africa's exposed coast. A sandbar built by waves and currents blocked the entrance, so breakwaters were built and the entrance dredged, allowing large ships by the early twentieth century; dredging continues and the channel was widened and deepened in the late 2000s. Its situation is the South African port closest by road and rail to Gauteng, about 600 km away, with a hinterland including KwaZulu-Natal, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, the Free State, North West and landlocked neighbours, and it lies on shipping routes between Asia, the Middle East and the Atlantic. It began as a trading settlement in 1824, grew with Natal's sugar industry from the 1850s and expanded after railways reached the Witwatersrand in the 1890s, and is managed by Transnet National Ports Authority.

questions.question: Describe the main terminals, exports and imports of the Port of Durban.
questions.expected_answer: The Durban Container Terminal, the largest in South Africa, has handled close to three million TEUs in a year, more than half of national container traffic, importing consumer goods, machinery, parts and chemicals mainly from Asia and Europe and exporting manufactured goods, processed food, chemicals and refrigerated fruit. One of Africa's largest car terminals exports South African-made vehicles, including from the Prospecton factory, mainly to Europe, and imports vehicles. Liquid bulk terminals such as Island View receive crude oil, petrol, diesel and chemicals, stored and sent inland mainly by pipeline. A bulk sugar terminal at Maydon Wharf exports raw sugar, and dry bulk and break-bulk include grain, minerals, timber, steel and machinery. The port also has fishing, ship repair and dry docks, a cruise terminal and a small craft harbour. Exports include vehicles, sugar, fruit, chemicals, manufactured goods and steel; imports include consumer goods, machinery, vehicles, fuel, crude oil, chemicals and sometimes grain; the port supports tens of thousands of jobs.

questions.question: Describe the specialised ships and transport links of the Port of Durban and one challenge it faces.
questions.expected_answer: Container ships are loaded by ship-to-shore gantry cranes and have grown so large that channels and berths had to be deepened; car carriers or ro-ro ships have internal decks and ramps; tankers connect to shore pipelines; bulk carriers load sugar or grain by conveyors or grabs; reefers carry chilled fruit, meat and fish; and tugboats and pilots guide ships through the entrance. The port is linked inland by road via the N3 to Pietermaritzburg and Gauteng and the N2 along the coast, with thousands of trucks daily; by rail along the Durban to Gauteng corridor with container trains to City Deep; by the multi-product fuel pipeline to Gauteng; and by air through King Shaka International Airport, allowing intermodal journeys without unpacking containers. Challenges include congestion and low efficiency from equipment breakdowns, ageing cranes, skills shortages and rail problems, causing ships to wait, addressed by new equipment and private partnerships; road congestion and pollution; lack of space, with plans for a dug-out port at the old airport site; and natural hazards such as the April 2022 floods.
